title: Two-Phase

post.author: u/key_safe_beatrix
post.title: I carry the keys for an estate agency after hours. At 21:00 three families sat in removal vans outside three houses, their money gone, no keys, and the record says nobody owns any of the houses.

blocks.text: I'm Beatrix, out-of-hours agent for an estate agency. On completion day, the day a house sale finishes, sellers leave their keys with us for the buyers. After 17:30 the office phone rings on mine, and the key safe rides in my car.

Friday 5 March was one chain: three sales linked, each depending on the next. The Uttleys were buying the Gathercoles' house, the Gathercoles the Tunnicliffes', and the Tunnicliffes a builder's new cottage. A chain finishes all together or not at all: not a majority, which means more than half, but all three.
The lead solicitor's firm runs it on a computer that answers other computers, called a server, with a program called the completion system.

First, it asks each buyer's bank in turn: ready? The banks are the parties, the ones who must act. A ready bank sets the money aside so it can't be spent twice: a hold. The family's banking app shows it as gone, though it hasn't moved.
A bank that has said ready has promised. It can't pay or let go until it's told which.

Second, once all three are ready, the system decides: commit, meaning go ahead with all three sales, or abort, meaning let every hold go, if any bank said no. It writes the decision down before telling anyone.

It writes it in a file of its decisions, its log, on the part of the server that keeps files with the power off: the disk. That's how it remembers after being switched off and on. Third, it tells everyone: the banks pay, my phone gets "completed" for each house, and I hand over keys.
The system also posts each step to a page agencies can read, on another computer. Each line: time, who, what happened.

16:58:04  Uttleys' bank        ready, money held
16:58:31  Gathercoles' bank    ready, money held
16:58:58  Tunnicliffes' bank   ready, money held
16:59:00  completion system    disk full: debug notes since Mon 1 Mar. retrying
16:59:40  completion system    restarted after a stop at 16:59:10. chain 3307: no decision. waiting for a person
Extra notes a program writes to help find a fault are switched on by a debug setting. Someone left it on from Monday 1 March, and by Friday the notes had filled the disk.
The decision usually follows about 2 seconds after the last ready. The system had never stopped inside them. A program stopping mid-job is called a crash. This one crashed at 16:59:10.

The system restarts itself after a crash. At 16:59:40 it found no decision in its log, so, as built, it stopped to wait for a person. Its alert went by email to a support inbox read in office hours; the firm's phones close at 17:00 on Fridays.
Our office had fielded the families' calls since five. From 17:31 to 17:40 my phone rang three times, one family each: money gone, no keys.
Three vans. Three houses. Three holds.
At 21:00 I drove past all three houses: a van outside each, a family in each cab, their keys in my car. On the agencies' page, all three houses read "owner: pending". Nobody owns any of them.

blocks.text: The banks can't decide alone: they promised. The system won't decide without a person, and nobody is reading. What should the firm change before its next chain?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Your firm's program has a name in the trade. The one that asks and decides is the coordinator. Asking everyone to promise, then deciding and telling, is called two-phase commit. Before you choose, read your list again. At 16:59:40, what did the coordinator still know about the three readies? What did each bank know about the other two? And if the coordinator had never come back, which of them could have finished the chain without guessing?

replies.author: u/key_safe_beatrix
replies.text: Nothing. Its log held no decision, and the readies were only in its memory, what a computer holds while it runs, gone with the crash. Each bank knew only its own ready. None of them could finish without guessing, so all three are still waiting.

comments.author: u/time_out_and_go_ethelred
comments.text: Every system that waits on another needs a timeout: a limit on how long it waits before acting on its own. If the coordinator goes quiet, each side should time out and go ahead; waiting forever is worse. Give each bank an hour. All three had said ready, so all three would have paid before 18:00, and those families would be asleep in their new houses tonight.

replies.author: u/key_safe_beatrix
replies.text: One of the dads said much the same at 21:00, standing by his van.

comments.author: u/sale_by_sale_domenica
comments.text: I'd give up on all together. Do it as a saga: one long job done as separate steps, each final on its own. Complete each sale in turn, bottom of the chain first. If a later sale fails, refund the earlier ones, in steps: the bank sends the buyer's money back, the buyer hands back the keys, and the house goes back to its seller. No bank ever sits on a promise.

reply.prompt: The firm's next chain completes on Friday 2 April. What should it change in its completion system before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Write the decision on three servers that agree by majority before telling anyone.
options.part2: On Monday 8 March the firm switched the debug setting off. Then it moved the completion system's record onto three servers in three different rooms. Each bank's ready is now stored on all three as it arrives. A decision counts only once two of the three have stored it, and nobody hears it before then. In the sim, replaying 5 March: server 1 fills its disk and crashes at 16:59:10, as before. At 16:59:15, after 5 seconds of silence, server 2 takes over. It finds all three readies on a majority, stores commit on two of three and tells everyone. All three sales are complete at 16:59:15, and no family's money is held for more than 0:01:11. With the Tunnicliffes' bank saying no instead, server 2 writes abort at 16:59:15 and every hold is let go. On 2 April the chain completed in the afternoon, and I handed over the keys before dark.
options.senior: Two-phase commit blocks because one machine holds the only copy of the decision. Once a party has promised, it can't decide alone, and if the coordinator dies before deciding, everyone waits. Don't fix the waiting by letting parties guess; fix the single copy. Store each party's ready and the decision on three servers that agree by majority, written there before anyone is told (Rule 1, for a group). Any surviving server can then read what was stored and finish: commit if every party said ready, abort if any didn't. That is Gray and Lamport's Paxos Commit; plain two-phase commit is its version with no spare. It costs one extra message delay and two more servers to run, and it still waits if two of the three are down at once.

options.text: Complete each sale in turn and refund a family if a later sale in the chain fails.
options.part2: The firm ran each sale on its own, bottom of the chain first, refunding the earlier ones if a later sale failed. In the sim, replaying 5 March: the Uttleys' sale completes at 16:58:04, the Gathercoles' at 16:58:31, the Tunnicliffes' at 16:58:58, and the crash at 16:59:10 finds nothing left to do. No money is held. But for 27 seconds the Gathercoles own no house, and then the Tunnicliffes. Now set the Tunnicliffes' bank to say no: two sales go through, and at 16:59:00 the runner must refund them. With the full disk it can't write the refunds, and at 21:00 the Tunnicliffes have sold their house and own no other, 4:01:29 after their sale. On 2 April every bank said yes, and the seconds in between passed unnoticed. Next time a refund may take days.
options.senior: A saga swaps blocking for a window. Each sale commits on its own, so no party sits on a promise and no money is held, which is why separate organisations often prefer it (s4e11). The price is isolation: between steps the world can see half a chain, a family that owns no house or two. If a later step fails, the earlier ones are undone by refunds, new steps that must themselves be written down and can themselves fail. Choose a saga when steps can be undone in business terms and a half-done state is tolerable. A house chain, where a family must not be left without a home, fits two-phase commit with the decision kept by a majority better.

options.text: If no decision arrives in an hour, let each party complete its own part on its own.
options.part2: The firm told each bank: if no decision comes within an hour of your ready, pay. In the sim, replaying 5 March: the Uttleys' bank pays at 17:58:04, the Gathercoles' at 17:58:31, the Tunnicliffes' at 17:58:58. All three sales complete, an hour late, and it looks like the answer. Now set the Tunnicliffes' bank to say no, as a bank will when mortgage money hasn't arrived. The other two banks never hear it. At 17:58 both go ahead and pay. Two sales complete and the third never does: the Tunnicliffes have sold their house and own no other, for 3:01:29 by 21:00. Nothing in the rule could tell the two banks that the third had said no.
options.senior: A party that has said ready has promised to do whatever the coordinator decides, and it doesn't know what that is. Going ahead after a timeout is a guess: right when everyone said ready, wrong when anyone said no, and the guessing party can't tell which. XA calls this a heuristic decision and warns it may leave shared resources inconsistent. A timeout is the right tool to notice that the coordinator has gone quiet, not to decide in its place. Keep the decision where another server can read it, so the wait is seconds, and never let a promised party decide alone.

options.text: After a crash, cancel the whole chain and run all three sales again from the start.
options.verdict: It can't tell who already acted
options.part2: The firm set the system to cancel the chain after any crash and run all three sales again. In the sim, replaying 5 March: at 16:59:40 it cancels, lets the three holds go and asks again. The disk is still full, so at 17:00:50 it crashes again before any decision, and again every 100 seconds: 145 reruns by 21:00. The families' apps flicker, money gone, back, gone, and the Uttleys' money is held for 3:52:16 of the night. Now set the crash to just after the decision is written, when the Uttleys' bank has already been told and paid. The restart can't cancel a payment already made, but it runs the chain again anyway, and at 17:00:30 the Uttleys' bank pays a second time.
options.senior: Starting again throws away the one thing that matters after a crash: what was decided, and who has already acted on it. If the crash came after anyone was told, cancelling contradicts a party that has already paid, and rerunning makes it pay twice. If the cause is still there, like a full disk, the rerun crashes the same way and the money is held again each time. A restart must read its log and finish what it decided. When it finds no decision, aborting is safe only because the decision is always written before anyone is told (XA's presumed rollback), and only if it can then write the abort.

sim.title: Replay completion day for chain 3307
sim.lede: You're Beatrix on Friday 5 March 2027 at 16:58:00, before the completion system asks anyone. As given data: it asks each buyer's bank in turn; the Uttleys' bank answers at 16:58:04, the Gathercoles' at 16:58:31, the Tunnicliffes' at 16:58:58. A ready bank puts a hold on the money. The decision is due 2 seconds after the last answer, at 16:59:00. That night the disk was full at 16:59:00; a failed write is retried for 10 seconds, so the crash comes at 16:59:10. One server restarts itself after 30 seconds; with three servers, a surviving server takes over after 5 seconds of silence. The go-ahead rule waits an hour. Saga mode uses only the crash, the Tunnicliffes' bank's answer and where its log is kept. Set the rules, then play 16:58:00 to 21:00:00.
sim.tryThis: Try this: play it as built: three holds still on at 21:00 and the Uttleys' money held 4:01:56. Three servers: server 2 finishes at 16:59:15, money held 0:01:11 at most. Go ahead after an hour: all three banks pay at 17:58; then make the Tunnicliffes' bank say no, and two sales complete while the Tunnicliffes own no house for 3:01:29. Cancel and run again: 145 reruns by 21:00, money held 3:52:16; with the crash just after the decision, the Uttleys pay twice. Saga mode: nothing held, 27 seconds with no house; with a no and the full disk, 4:01:29.

explain.oneLine: Nothing at the firm took the money. The completion system crashed in the 2 seconds between the last ready and writing its decision, and two-phase commit gives a bank that has promised no way to decide alone. With the only copy of the decision on one server, every bank waited for a person.

steps.title: Two-phase commit, step by step.
steps.text: The coordinator, here the completion system, runs changes that must all happen or none. First, prepare: it asks each party, here each buyer's bank, whether it can do its part. A party that can makes its part safe, writes its promise to its own disk, then answers ready; for a bank, that is the hold. What goes wrong here: a party that answers before writing its promise can forget it in a restart. Second, decide: when every party is ready the coordinator chooses commit, and if any says no it chooses abort. It writes the decision in its log before anything else (Rule 1). Third, tell: it sends the decision to every party, and each pays or lets go. What goes wrong here: a party that never hears the decision waits.

steps.title: Why everyone waited: a promise with nobody to keep it.
steps.text: Between saying ready and hearing the decision, a party is in doubt. It has promised to pay if told commit and to let go if told abort, and it can't know which, because only the coordinator knows whether every other party said ready. If the coordinator dies after the readies and before the decision, every party that promised must wait. That is the blocking problem. On 5 March the window was about 2 seconds, 16:58:58 to 16:59:00, and a debug setting left on since Monday filled the disk inside it. The system retried for 10 seconds, crashed at 16:59:10, came back at 16:59:40 with no decision in its log and stopped for a person, who was not reading. What goes wrong: the longer nobody acts, the longer the holds stay. At 21:00 the Uttleys' money had been held for 4:01:56.

steps.title: Two tempting cures that break things.
steps.text: Letting each party go ahead after a timeout turns the wait into a guess. On 5 March all three had said ready, so going ahead at 17:58 happens to work. If the Tunnicliffes' bank had said no, the other two would still go ahead and pay, and the chain would end half done: two sales complete and the Tunnicliffes with no house. XA calls a party deciding alone a heuristic decision and warns it may leave things inconsistent. Cancelling and rerunning after every crash ignores the log. It can't tell who already acted, so a bank that had paid pays twice; and if the cause is still there, like a full disk, it crashes again, 145 times by 21:00.

steps.title: The fix: keep the decision where a majority keeps it.
steps.text: Put the record on three servers that agree by majority, as the beekeepers' servers did in s8e04. First, each bank's ready is stored on the three servers as it arrives. Second, the decision counts only once two of the three have stored it, and only then is anyone told (Rule 1, for a group). Third, if the server running the chain goes quiet for 5 seconds, another takes over, reads what a majority stored and finishes: commit if all three said ready, abort if any didn't. On 5 March that is 16:59:15, with money held for 0:01:11 at most. Gray and Lamport call this Paxos Commit; plain two-phase commit is its version with no spare server. What goes wrong: if two of the three servers are down at once, it waits too.

steps.title: Sagas: no waiting, a different price.
steps.text: A saga, from s4e11, runs each sale as its own step, final as soon as it is done, and undoes earlier steps with refunds if a later one fails. Nothing is held and nobody waits. But between steps a family can own no house or two: on 5 March the Gathercoles own none for 27 seconds, then the Tunnicliffes. If the cottage sale fails, the refunds are new steps that must be written and done, and with a full disk they can't be: the Tunnicliffes would own no house for 4:01:29. Choose a saga when steps can be undone in business terms and a half-done state is tolerable.

diagram.aria: The fix replayed for 5 March. The completion system on server 1 asks the three banks ready at 16:58:00; all three are ready by 16:58:58, and each ready is copied to servers 2 and 3. At 16:59:10 server 1 crashes with a full disk and no decision. At 16:59:15, after 5 seconds of silence, server 2 takes over, stores commit on 2 of 3 servers and tells the banks to pay. Outcome: all three sales complete at 16:59:15.

explain.caption: The fix, replayed for 5 March. The three readies are copied to servers 2 and 3 as they arrive. Server 1 fills its disk and crashes at 16:59:10, before any decision. After 5 seconds of silence server 2 takes over, finds all three readies on a majority, stores commit on 2 of 3 and tells every bank. All three sales are complete at 16:59:15.

fix.title: The fix: store every ready and the decision on three servers that agree by majority
fix.text: Switch the debug setting off and watch disk space. Then move the completion system's record onto three servers in separate places. Store each bank's ready on all three as it arrives. Count a decision only once two of the three have stored it, and tell nobody before then. If the server running the chain goes quiet for 5 seconds, another takes over, reads the record and finishes: commit if every bank said ready, abort if any said no. Keep the banks waiting for the decision, never guessing; with a survivor ready to finish, the wait is seconds, not a night. Each bank must also write its own ready to its own disk before answering, so its own restart can't forget the promise.

limits: It still waits if two of the three servers are down at once. A majority moves the risk; it doesn't remove waiting.
It costs one extra message delay on every chain, and two more servers to run, update and watch.
It protects the decision, not the parties. A bank that forgets its own ready after a restart can still break the chain.

explain.seniorTake: Two-phase commit is the honest way to make several parties act as one: everyone promises, one place decides and writes it down, then everyone is told. Its weakness is not the steps but the single copy of the decision. A party that has promised must not decide alone, so when the only coordinator dies between the promises and the decision, everyone waits for it, or for a person. The cure is not a timeout, a rerun or a guess. It is to keep the promises and the decision where a majority of servers keeps them, so any survivor can finish: that is Paxos Commit, and it costs one message delay. When the parties are separate organisations that won't hold a promise open, use a saga instead, and bound the half-done window it brings.

realWorld.title: XA, 1991: two-phase commit as a standard
realWorld.text: X/Open's XA specification defines how a transaction manager (TM), the coordinator, talks to resource managers (RMs), the parties, such as databases. It says: "TMs and RMs use two-phase commit with presumed rollback". Of phase one: "This asks whether the RM can guarantee its ability to commit the transaction branch." A party that can answers yes only after "it records stably the information it needs to do so".

realWorld.title: XA: decide and write, then tell
realWorld.text: Of phase two: "(Before issuing requests to commit, the TM stably records the fact that it decided to commit, as well as a list of all involved RMs.)" That is Rule 1 for the coordinator: the decision is written before anyone hears it.

realWorld.title: XA: when a party decides alone
realWorld.text: XA's name for the go-ahead rule is a heuristic decision: "an RM that has prepared to commit a transaction branch may decide to commit or roll back its work independently of the TM. It could then unlock shared resources. This may leave them in an inconsistent state."

realWorld.title: The Open Group catalogue: C193
realWorld.text: The Open Group lists the specification as C193, Distributed TP: The XA Specification, dated 1 February 1992, and says it defines "the interface between two of them, the transaction manager and local resource manager."

realWorld.title: Gray and Lamport: the blocking problem
realWorld.text: Jim Gray and Leslie Lamport open their abstract with the problem in one line: "The classic Two-Phase Commit protocol blocks if the coordinator fails."

realWorld.title: Gray and Lamport: a majority instead
realWorld.text: "Fault-tolerant consensus algorithms also reach agreement, but do not block whenever any majority of the processes are working." Their Paxos Commit runs that kind of agreement on each party's commit-or-abort answer.

realWorld.title: Gray and Lamport: the cost
realWorld.text: "In the fault-free case, this algorithm requires one extra message delay but has the same stable-storage write delay as Two-Phase Commit." Plain two-phase commit is the version with no spare coordinators.

realWorld.title: Published in 2006
realWorld.text: Microsoft Research's publication page lists the paper in ACM Transactions on Database Systems, volume 31, issue 1, 2006, pages 133 to 160.

asked: Why does two-phase commit block, and what fixes it?
When would you choose a saga instead?
interview.answer: Two-phase commit makes several parties, say a payments database and a stock database, commit one change together. Phase one, prepare: the coordinator asks each party whether it can commit; a party that can makes its part safe, writes its promise to its own disk and answers ready. Phase two: when all are ready the coordinator writes commit in its log, or abort if any said no, and only then tells everyone, who commit or roll back. It blocks because a party that has promised can't decide alone: it doesn't know what the others answered. If the coordinator dies after the promises and before the decision, every party waits, holding its locks or money, until the coordinator returns or a person acts. A timeout that lets parties go ahead breaks all-or-nothing, and restarting from scratch can't tell who already acted. The fix is to keep the promises and the decision on several machines that agree by majority, Gray and Lamport's Paxos Commit, so any survivor can finish; plain two-phase commit is its version with no spare. It costs one extra message delay. I'd choose a saga instead when the parties are separate organisations that won't hold a promise open, or the work spans minutes or days, and each step can be undone in business terms; the price is a visible half-done window and refunds that must themselves succeed. I'd tell the story of a house chain whose completion system crashed at 16:59:10, two seconds from commit, and held three families' money for over four hours.

atWork: Look for a single coordinator whose crash leaves resources held until someone steps in. A common pattern is a payments or bookings service that runs two-phase commit, through an XA transaction manager or a home-made 'reserve, then confirm' flow, on one machine with its decision log on one disk. Read-only checks are enough. First, find where the decision is written and how many machines hold it. Second, ask what happens if that machine dies between the parties' readies and the decision: who is alerted, who can finish, and how long holds or locks stay in place. Third, check the parties' rules: does any of them time out and go ahead alone, and does a restart read its log or start again? In AWS, look for an XA transaction manager on a single EC2 instance, and for reserve-then-confirm flows whose state lives in one place. Standards: if your company is pursuing ISO 9001:2015, clause 8.5.1 (control of production and service provision) expects processes to run under controlled conditions, and a completion that can stall for hours with no named person to finish it is a gap. If it is pursuing a SOC 2 report that covers processing integrity (PI1), the criteria expect processing to be complete and accurate, so write down how an in-doubt transaction is finished and by whom. Flag for the design: a coordinator with one copy of its decision, or parties that decide alone after a timeout, would need rework before an audit, so put the recovery path into the design from the first draft.

recall.prompt: Your company's checkout changes a stock database and a payments database together, through two-phase commit run by a single coordinator. In a failure test, the coordinator's machine is switched off just after both databases answered prepared. What happens to the stock and the customer's card, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: Both databases have promised and can't decide alone, so the stock and the card hold stay held until the coordinator returns or a person acts
Keep the decision on several machines that agree by majority (Paxos Commit or a consensus store), so a survivor can finish
Write each promise and the decision to disk before anyone is told (Rule 1)

recall.model: Both databases answered prepared, so each has promised: the stock is reserved and the card hold is on, and neither can decide alone, because the other might have been told commit or abort. With the only coordinator switched off before it decided, both stay held until the coordinator comes back or a person acts. That's two-phase commit's blocking problem. I'd keep the decision, and each prepared answer, on three machines that agree by majority, Paxos Commit or a consensus store such as etcd, written there before anyone is told (Rule 1), so if the coordinator dies, a surviving machine reads the record and finishes in seconds. Each database must also write its promise to its own disk before answering, so its own restart can't forget it.

recall.prompt: In the sim, with the 16:59:10 crash as that night and everything else as built, which one change finishes all three sales within seconds?
options: Banks go ahead and pay after an hour with no decision
The decision stored on three servers, counted once 2 of 3 store it
After a restart, cancel the whole chain and run all three sales again
Saga mode, with the Tunnicliffes' bank saying no
recall.why: Server 2 takes over at 16:59:15, finds all three readies on a majority, stores commit and tells everyone: all three sales complete, money held 0:01:11 at most. Going ahead waits an hour; cancelling and rerunning with the full disk crashes 145 times; the saga with a no leaves the Tunnicliffes with no house.

recall.prompt: In an interview you're asked: walk me through two-phase commit. Why does it block, and what fixes it?

keyIdeas.idea: Phase one: the coordinator asks each party to prepare, and each makes its part safe and promises. Phase two: the coordinator writes commit or abort, then tells everyone
A party that has promised can't decide alone; if the coordinator dies before deciding, everyone waits
Keep the promises and the decision on several machines that agree by majority (Paxos Commit), so a survivor finishes

recall.model: Two-phase commit makes several parties commit one change together. Phase one: the coordinator asks each party to prepare; a party that can makes its part safe, writes its promise to its own disk and answers ready. Phase two: when all are ready, the coordinator writes commit in its log, or abort if any said no, and then tells everyone. It blocks because a party that has promised can't decide alone: it doesn't know what the others answered. If the coordinator dies after the promises and before the decision, every party is in doubt and everyone waits, holding locks or money, until it returns or a person acts. The fix is to keep the promises and the decision on several machines that agree by majority, Gray and Lamport's Paxos Commit, so a survivor can read them and finish. It costs one extra message delay.

recall.prompt: When is a saga usually a better choice than two-phase commit?
options: When every step must take effect at the same instant or not at all
When the steps belong to separate organisations that won't hold a promise open, and each can be undone by a refund
When the coordinator runs on only one server
When all the parties share one database
recall.why: A saga commits each step on its own and undoes earlier ones with compensations, such as refunds, so nobody holds a promise open. The price is a half-done window. Two-phase commit suits steps that must be all or nothing at once; one shared database needs only an ordinary transaction.

recall.prompt: Why can't a bank that has answered ready simply decide for itself after an hour of silence?
options: Banks are not allowed to use timers
Another bank may have said no, or the coordinator may have decided, and a guess can break all-or-nothing
Deciding would make the coordinator crash again
A hold can only be released by a person
recall.why: A bank that said ready doesn't know what the others answered or what the coordinator decided. Going ahead is a guess: in the sim, with the Tunnicliffes' bank saying no, the other two pay at 17:58 and the chain ends half done. XA calls this a heuristic decision.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 2 months later. The three servers have held all spring: two crashes, both finished by a survivor within seconds. Then on Friday 30 April 2027 a two-sale chain stuck. One buyer's bank, a small building society, answered ready at 15:02:12. Its own server restarted for an update at 15:02:20. At 15:02:31 the decision, commit, stored on two of three servers, reached it. It had no record of the chain, refused to pay and let the hold go. The other sale completed. One family has keys; the other has its money back and no house.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to Beatrix. The decision was safe on three servers, so how did one sale complete and the other not, and what must the society change?

keyIdeas.idea: The society answered ready without writing its promise to its own disk, so its restart forgot it
A party must write its ready and its hold to disk before answering: Rule 1 for every party
On restart, a party with a promise on record keeps the hold and asks for the decision instead of letting go

coldCase.model: The coordinator's side was safe; the society's wasn't. It answered ready at 15:02:12, but its promise and the hold were only in memory, not written to its own disk, so the restart at 15:02:20 forgot them. When commit arrived at 15:02:31 it had no record, refused to pay and let the hold go, and the chain ended half done. Two-phase commit needs Rule 1 at every party: write the ready and the hold to its own disk before answering, as XA says a resource manager records stably what it needs, then replies. On restart, a party that finds a promise on record keeps the hold and asks for the decision, waiting in doubt rather than guessing. Test it by restarting a bank between its ready and the decision.
